classification.difficultyReason: Combines two similarity proofs and corresponding-side ratios to establish a further relationship.

content.prompt: In the diagram to the right, the line $CE$ and the line $FH$ are tangents to both circles with centres $P$ and $Q$. The points of tangency for $CE$ are $C$ and $D$, and the points of tangency for $FH$ are $F$ and $H$.

spec.description: Two unshaded circles with external common tangent C–D–E, internal common tangent F–G–H, and collinear centres P–G–Q–E. Coordinates determine exact tangency; no numerical dimensions are displayed. Ordinary source blue lines and red point markers become black under house style.
spec.mathematics: PC=PF and QD=QH are circle radii; PC and QD are perpendicular to CE, while PF and QH are perpendicular to FH. Radii are not drawn in the question figure.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied circles, tangents, line of centres, points and labels are visible; no proof annotations or right-angle marks are added.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Prove that $\triangle CPE$ is similar to $\triangle DQE$.

answer.short: $\angle PCE=\angle QDE=90^\circ$ and $\angle CEP=\angle DEQ$. Therefore $\triangle CPE\sim\triangle DQE$ (AA).
answer.worked:
Join $PC$ and $QD$. A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at its point of contact, so $\angle PCE=\angle QDE=90^\circ$.

Since $C,D,E$ are collinear and $P,Q,E$ are collinear, $\angle CEP=\angle DEQ$ (the same angle at $E$).

Therefore $\triangle CPE\sim\triangle DQE$ (AA).

children.label: b
children.prompt: Prove that $\triangle GFP$ is similar to $\triangle GHQ$.

answer.short: $\angle GFP=\angle GHQ=90^\circ$ and $\angle FGP=\angle HGQ$ (vertically opposite). Therefore $\triangle GFP\sim\triangle GHQ$ (AA).
answer.worked:
Join $PF$ and $QH$. A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at its point of contact, so $\angle GFP=\angle GHQ=90^\circ$.

The lines $FH$ and $PQ$ intersect at $G$, so $\angle FGP=\angle HGQ$ (vertically opposite angles).

Therefore $\triangle GFP\sim\triangle GHQ$ (AA).

From part a, corresponding sides give
$$\frac{CE}{DE}=\frac{CP}{DQ}.$$
From part b, corresponding sides give
$$\frac{FG}{GH}=\frac{PF}{QH}.$$
Since $CP=PF$ and $DQ=QH$ (radii of their respective circles),
$$\frac{CE}{DE}=\frac{FG}{GH}.$$
Therefore
$$\begin{align*}CE\times GH&=DE\times FG,\\\frac{CE}{FG}&=\frac{DE}{GH}.\end{align*}$$
